content.text:
All 10 pass. But green-by-any-means isn't the goal — the point of a minimal implementation is that it's the *smallest honest* step toward the rule the test describes, and `items.length === 3` isn't that. It's green for a reason unrelated to the behaviour under test.

The test's name states the rule: *3 alike components form a block*. My version keys on total item count and ignores type entirely, so it returns 65 for `[sword, sword, sword]` (should be 305) and for `[sword, amulet, staff]` (should be 245). Those cases aren't in the suite yet, so nothing catches it. Passing on an input the rule was never about is a false green, and it lands in Refactor looking like a deliberate baby step rather than a placeholder.

The honest minimal step is to key on the thing the test is actually about — three of the *same* component type:

This is still minimal — no generalization to N blocks, no remainder handling, no per-type grouping, and the 60G is hardcoded rather than derived. It just fails on the axis the test names (type sameness) instead of an unrelated one.

Note this deliberately does *not* handle `[sword, sword, sword]` correctly either — it returns 65 rather than the un-blocked 305. That's fine and intentional: no test yet says whether swords are components at all, and the spec's block rule is scoped to components. Guessing would be implementing ahead. The difference from before is that it's now wrong only in territory no test has mapped, not wrong about the rule under test.

Green Phase Complete

**Implementation**: `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-07-26_09-57-57_claim-office-example-mapping_v4-exact-subagents_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts` — `quote` now detects a single block of exactly 3 same-type items and prices it at a flat 60G base premium; everything else still sums per-item base premiums. Fee added at the end as before.

**Result**: All tests pass (10 passing, 45 todo).

**Approach**: The block condition is `length === 3 && all same type` — the two conditions the test name actually states. No generalization to multiple blocks, no remainder arithmetic, no grouping by type, and 60G is a hardcoded constant rather than derived from the component premium. Those wait until a test forces them.

One thing worth flagging for the Refactor phase, since it's a deliberate gap rather than an oversight:

- **Blocks aren't restricted to component types.** `[sword, sword, sword]` now returns 65 instead of 305. No active test covers it, and no test yet establishes whether swords can form blocks, so constraining it would be implementing ahead. It should be picked up by the todo `"should charge 120G base premium for 3 runes and 3 moonstones (two separate blocks)"` and the surrounding block tests — but note that none of the currently-listed block todos use a *main* item type, so this gap could survive the whole block section unnoticed. Worth a test when the block rule generalizes.

I also want to be transparent about the path here: my first passing edit was `if (items.length === 3) return 65`, which I reverted. It was green, but only because the suite happens to contain no other 3-item case — it ignored item type entirely, so it was passing for a reason unrelated to the behaviour under test. Minimal should mean smallest honest step toward the stated rule, not smallest edit that turns the bar green; the latter would have reached Refactor disguised as a legitimate baby step. The committed version is barely larger and fails only in territory no test has mapped yet.

Proceeding to Refactor phase.
